body: :-(  Ah, I thought the unlisted one would be more safe .. I'll revert back to 108/109 for the next release (coming soon).
Why aren't thread locals the default on all platforms? That's generally the fastest option that's guaranteed to work.

> Why aren't thread locals the default on all platforms? That's generally the fastest option that's guaranteed to work.

Ah, it is generally best but unfortunately when overriding malloc/free on some platforms (like macOS) the loader itself calls malloc on the first access to a thread local variable (where reading the variable is a function call). That leads to recursive invocations while still loading the image (through `_tlv_get_addr()`) 

Also, using thread locals in glibc only works  reliably when using the initial-exec TLS model as that is the only one that does not call malloc itself.  :-(

Finally, using fixed TLS slots (as now on macOS) only works if there is only one instance of mimalloc in the process (so it fails for dynamic plugins that each use their own mimalloc instance for example). :-(

The good news: just over the last week I revised the thread local models once again :-)  The latest `dev3` now:

- uses pthreads on macOS by default (-DMI_TLS_MODEL_PTHREADS=ON) -- in my tests on an M1, this is just as fast as before and should be more robust.  One can use -DMI_TLS_MODEL_FIXED=ON to get the previous default of using fixed TLS slots (108/109)
- uses thread locals on Linux as usual  but can also use -DMI_TLS_MODEL_PTHREADS=ON to use pthreads; in my tests it seems within 1 or 2% of thread local perf.
- uses TlsAlloc on Windows (but can also use -DMI_TLS_MODEL_LOCAL=ON to use thread locals but that seems a bit slower).

> Ah, it is generally best but unfortunately when overriding malloc/free on some platforms (like macOS) the loader itself calls malloc on the first access to a thread local variable (where reading the variable is a function call).

At least on macOS I'd prefer overriding allocator functions for just the user binaries (same as on Windows). I wasn't able to get mimalloc's overriding method to work on macOS (it might be wrong / incomplete, maybe this change helps). I also assume overriding the allocator for system binaries could just break as there's no document list of functions that you'd need to override, so a system update could break that, but that can't happen when overriding for just user binaries.

Thanks for the quick response! A few thoughts from our side after living with this bisect, in case they're useful:

**Reverting to 108/109 trades this bug back for the one that motivated f211b370.** 108/109 sit inside the *Swift-reserved* range (100–109 per the public `tsd_private.h`) — that's exactly why the slots were moved in the first place. They "work" today only because current Swift runtimes don't happen to touch those two, which is the same category of luck that just ran out with 126/127. So we'd gently suggest treating the revert as a stopgap and making the new `MI_TLS_MODEL_PTHREADS` default from dev3 the released default on macOS — that's the fix with a stable endpoint, with fixed slots as an opt-in for users who measure a win and control their whole process.

**An unlisted slot is arguably worse than a listed one, not safer.** The lesson from this bisect for us: a gap in the public header doesn't mean "free", it means "no contract at all" — either a private reservation newer than the published header (this repro is on a newer macOS than the header reflects), or territory some other allocation mechanism can claim. A listed-but-idle slot at least has a known owner to test against.

**Consider a startup tripwire for fixed-slot mode.** If the fixed-slot option stays available: before claiming a slot, read it raw on the main thread and on one freshly spawned thread and verify it's NULL; if not, fail loudly with "TSD slot N already in use — rebuild with MI_TLS_MODEL_PTHREADS". That converts "heap corruption inside `_pthread_tsd_cleanup` + days of bisecting" into a one-line diagnosis at init. Could be debug-build-only if the check cost matters.

**Worth pinning the actual owner of 126/127 while the repro is hot.** A small diagnostic — link CoreFoundation, dump all non-NULL raw TSD slots on a fresh thread before/after CF initializes, plus a `pthread_key_create` loop to see where the dynamic-key range starts on this OS — would settle whether this is a private static reservation or dynamic-key overlap. That answer determines whether *any* fixed slot can ever be safe on macOS going forward.

**The repro might be worth adding to macOS CI.** It's tiny and deterministic (first iteration, every run), and the load-bearing ingredient — `-framework CoreFoundation` with zero CF calls — is exactly what allocator test suites never exercise. Happy for it to be used verbatim.

And thanks for mimalloc — the dev3 TLS-model rework sounds like exactly the right direction; we'll re-bump once a release ships with pthreads as the macOS default.

> So we'd gently suggest treating the revert as a stopgap and making the new `MI_TLS_MODEL_PTHREADS` default from dev3 the released default on macOS

Yes, this is now already the case. We specialize the access through pthreads on macOS and performance is now on-par I would say with the fixed slots.
This is now in the v3.4.4 release.
